cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the structure holds because you are in it.
cells.act: ask the question you do not know the answer to
cells.ask: Before you lock a pattern into place, ask something you genuinely don't know. Ask it of someone, or hold it open alone, and let what comes back reshape what you build.
cells.core:
You are moving and the ground is coming with you. When you set a boundary, it holds. When you charge, the shape of the work changes. You act instead of just organizing, and the test is small and plain: a meeting goes the way you meant it to, and no correction is needed afterward.
The next thing this can feed is knowing less and seeing more. Before you lock a pattern this week, ask something you don't already know. Let the answer land without arguing with it. The structure will still be yours to set — but it will be set on what is actually there. That is what keeps it from going stale.

cells.tense: You are already bracing, already planning the move you have not made yet.
cells.act: cut to the logic and act on it
cells.ask: Take a decision you're circling. Strip it to its logic on a single page — what's true, what follows. Act on that once.
cells.core:
You have run the next three moves in your head before you have made the first one. The charge is real, and it has gone past the ground it was meant to move. Conversations get pre-decided. Structures get built before anyone sees the problem, so the thing you organize is not the one at hand — it is the one you braced for. People can feel the speed and step back from it.
Bring the charge down to the size of one clear thought. Take the decision you are circling and cut it to its logic — what is true, what follows — then act on that and stop. Not a plan for the quarter, a single move. You will still be pacing the room, just not the facts.

cells.tense: You were moving once, and now you are standing behind a door that already closed.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Choose one structure — a schedule, a room, a standing arrangement — and change one real thing about it. Small, physical, visible. Then stop.
cells.core:
The impulse to organize is still there, but it is not reaching your hands. You know what structure should look like; you can see the shape of it clearly. What you are not doing is starting. Time passes, the pattern stays the way it was, and you stand at the edge of it wondering why the charge that used to be here is not arriving. This is not a lack of ideas. It is a lack of motion.
Do not wait for the charge to come back first. Move one piece of the structure a single real inch — the shelf, the calendar, the way a standing thing is done — and stop there for now. Small and physical, done this week. The steady kind of change the record points to does not need momentum to start. It builds it.

cells.tense: You are writing the room and calling it the room being like that.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Look at the structure and find the piece that has finished. End it on purpose this week — cancel it, close it, take it down. Keep everything else exactly as it is.
cells.core:
The structure around you is not an accident. You shaped it — by deciding what stayed, what changed, who was included, what the pattern would be. And when someone asks how it got that way, the answer is that things just run like this. The hand that set the boundaries is not in the story. Meanwhile the charge keeps moving, and it is still yours.
Take one piece of the structure and look at whether it has finished its work. If it has, end it deliberately — cancel it, close it, take it down — because a structure that keeps what is done is not being held by anyone. Then look at what remains and know you are the one keeping it. That is the whole move: knowing which is which.
